title: Debt Covenant Recovery Plan
summary: Stabilizing lender confidence when EBITDA, liquidity, or covenant cushion deteriorates.
definition: A Debt Covenant Recovery Plan is the operating and lender-management response used when a leveraged portfolio company approaches or breaches covenant limits.
whyItMatters: PE cares because covenant pressure can transfer negotiating power to lenders, restrict strategic flexibility, and damage equity value.
commonProblems: Management sees covenant pressure too late.
Forecasts lack enough detail to support lender confidence.
Cash actions are scattered and not tied to covenant recovery.
diagnosticQuestions: Which covenant is under pressure and what is the true cushion by month?
What operating misses caused the pressure: EBITDA, cash, working capital, or debt?
What lender message can be supported by specific actions and dates?
dataNeeded: Monthly EBITDA, debt, cash, and liquidity forecast
Working capital detail and covenant sensitivity model
process: Calculate covenant cushion under base, downside, and severe downside cases.
Build a recovery bridge from operating actions to covenant improvement.
Install weekly cash and KPI command center.
Prepare lender communication, waiver, amendment, or equity cure options.
Track recovery actions until cushion is restored.
ebitdaLogic: The playbook protects equity by preserving lender flexibility, preventing forced value leakage, and restoring operating performance before debt terms become punitive.
caseExample: A sponsor-backed manufacturer facing leverage covenant pressure launches a cash war room, reduces inventory purchases, accelerates collections, freezes discretionary spend, and secures an amendment with a credible recovery package.
hundredDayPlan: Days 1-30: calculate true covenant exposure, install cash war room, identify immediate liquidity actions.
Days 31-60: execute EBITDA and working capital actions, engage lenders with evidence-backed plan.
Days 61-100: finalize amendment or waiver path, prove forecast accuracy, rebuild cushion.
commonMistakes: Treating lender communication as a finance-only exercise.
Using optimistic forecasts without operating owners behind the recovery.
Waiting for an actual breach before preparing amendment options.

  A[Covenant Pressure] --> B[Recovery Plan]

articleSections.title: Establish the Covenant and Liquidity Baseline
body: Start with the executed credit agreement, amendments, compliance certificates, lender model, and borrowing-base mechanics—not management's shorthand. Counsel and the CFO should create a definition ledger for debt, cash netting, permitted add-backs, pro forma synergies, fixed charges, baskets, cure rights, testing dates, and reporting deadlines. Recalculate the last two certificates from source ledgers and tie debt to lender statements. A recovery plan built on an ineligible add-back or misunderstood cure provision can turn a manageable miss into an unexpected default.

Build a test-date headroom schedule that separates contractual EBITDA from reported EBITDA and liquidity from accounting cash. For a company with $72 million of net debt, $16 million of covenant EBITDA, and a 5.0x maximum leverage ratio, leverage is 4.50x and debt capacity is $80 million, leaving $8 million of headroom. If the next-quarter forecast falls to $14 million, permitted debt drops to $70 million and the company breaches by $2 million unless debt is repaid, eligible EBITDA is restored, or an amendment changes the test. Show the math in dollars and turns so operators understand the consequence of forecast movement.

Liquidity analysis must run alongside covenant analysis because a technical cure can still leave the company unable to fund payroll or suppliers. Reconcile unrestricted cash, revolver availability, borrowing-base reserves, blocked accounts, overdue payables, tax obligations, and minimum operating cash by legal entity. The treasurer owns daily sources and uses; the CFO certifies weekly liquidity; the sponsor reviews covenant headroom and available cash together. Freeze distributions, acquisitions, and discretionary capital when either measure crosses an approved trigger rather than waiting for a formal breach.
articleSections.callout: Covenant headroom is not an accounting ratio; it is the dollar amount of forecast error the capital structure can still absorb.

articleSections.title: Make the 13-Week Cash Forecast the Control Tower
body: Construct the 13-week forecast from customer-level receipts and vendor, payroll, tax, interest, rent, and capital disbursements by bank account. Do not spread the annual budget into weeks. Collections leaders confirm invoice-level timing; procurement identifies critical suppliers and payment constraints; HR and tax owners certify fixed dates. The opening balance must tie to bank statements and the ending balance must reconcile to revolver draws and availability. Finance records forecast-to-actual variance by cause every Monday and updates assumptions only after explaining the miss.

Run base, downside, and severe cases with explicit operating drivers. The base case may use current collections and approved cost actions; downside can delay the largest three receipts by two weeks and reduce orders 10%; severe downside can add a customer loss, inventory write-down, or borrowing-base reserve. Show minimum liquidity, draw timing, and covenant impact in each case. A decision gate activates when downside liquidity falls below the minimum cash buffer or forecast accuracy exceeds a defined error band, forcing capital actions before optionality disappears.

A useful forecast changes behavior. The CEO chairs a twice-weekly cash war room during acute pressure, with the CFO as process owner and functional executives responsible for named inflows and outflows. No purchase order, hire, bonus, settlement, or capital project above set thresholds proceeds outside the forecast. This is not permanent centralized micromanagement: thresholds should relax after eight to twelve weeks of stable liquidity and forecast accuracy. Without a sunset rule, emergency controls can damage supplier trust, customer delivery, and management accountability long after the immediate risk passes.

articleSections.title: Sequence Operating, Working-Capital, and Capital Responses
body: Prioritize actions by speed, certainty, reversibility, and damage to enterprise value. First protect cash without impairing the franchise: accelerate valid collections, enforce milestone billing, stop speculative inventory, recover pricing leakage, and pause discretionary spend. Next execute structural EBITDA actions supported by operational detail, such as labor scheduling, footprint consolidation, procurement resets, or exit from negative-contribution work. Do not count a benefit twice in cash and EBITDA, and do not claim annualized savings as covenant EBITDA unless the agreement permits the add-back and the action is actually implemented.

Capital responses fill the remaining gap. Model revolver usage, asset sales, sale-leasebacks, subordinated capital, sponsor equity, and amendment economics against the same downside case. In the $72 million debt example, a $3 million permanent EBITDA recovery creates $15 million of capacity at 5.0x, while a $4 million equity cure may reduce net debt by only $4 million and could be limited in frequency or application. The recovery action is therefore more valuable if credible and timely, but equity may be the prudent bridge when execution cannot mature before the test date.

Failure modes include cutting customer-facing capacity faster than demand, stretching critical vendors until supply stops, assuming receivable acceleration repeats indefinitely, and pursuing an asset sale that consumes management attention without closing. Each action needs a downside consequence and rollback owner. The steering committee approves actions at weekly gates using realized cash, service levels, backlog, and covenant effect. An intervention that improves the ratio but destroys the order book merely moves the breach into a later quarter.

articleSections.title: Control Lender Sequencing and Recovery Governance
body: Contact lenders before a surprise certificate, but only after facts and asks are coherent. The first package should state the variance, corrected forecast, current liquidity, headroom by test date, actions underway, sponsor support position, and the precise relief requested. Sequence the agent bank first, then the broader syndicate in accordance with the agreement; keep counsel involved so oral discussion does not inadvertently waive rights or create inconsistent disclosure. A short factual update every week is more credible than occasional optimistic presentations.

Evaluate waiver, amendment, covenant reset, equity cure, and forbearance as distinct decisions. Compare fees, pricing step-ups, minimum liquidity, reporting burden, restricted payments, board observation, additional collateral, and future flexibility. Obtain investment-committee authority for a negotiating range before lender discussions. Management should not promise sponsor equity or accept operating constraints without approval. The board's restructuring or finance committee owns the decision log; the CFO owns information delivery; counsel tracks conditions precedent and deadlines.

Trust is built through cadence and forecast accuracy. Provide the same KPI definitions internally and externally, reconcile changes to prior submissions, and identify misses before the lender does. The board reviews weekly until base and downside cases both show adequate cushion through at least two test dates. Escalation occurs if liquidity misses by more than the approved tolerance, an action slips, or an add-back becomes disputed. Governance should also protect management capacity by assigning one lender workstream lead instead of allowing every executive to answer overlapping diligence requests.

articleSections.title: Validate the Cure and Return to Normalized Reporting
body: A signed waiver is a bridge, not proof of recovery. Finance should maintain a benefit ledger that ties every action to cash, reported EBITDA, covenant EBITDA, one-time cost, and supporting evidence. Savings are recognized after invoices, payroll, or run-rate activity confirms them; working-capital releases are not labeled recurring EBITDA. Recalculate headroom monthly under actual, base, and downside performance. In the example, $2.4 million of validated EBITDA recovery and $3 million of debt paydown produce $69 million of net debt and $16.4 million of covenant EBITDA, or 4.21x leverage and $13 million of capacity at 5.0x.

Normalize reporting only after the company achieves a defined gate: no reporting defaults, minimum liquidity maintained, forecast variance within tolerance, covenant compliance under downside, and operating service metrics stable for multiple cycles. Then move from twice-weekly cash reviews to weekly, and eventually to the normal monthly close and board cadence. Preserve the 13-week capability and action ledger so it can reactivate quickly. If controls vanish immediately after a cure, forecast discipline usually decays and the lender recognizes the recovery as temporary.

Exit and refinancing proof should include the definition ledger, historical certificates, forecast-accuracy trend, amendment terms, action-level benefit evidence, normalized working capital, and a bridge from reported to covenant EBITDA. Underwriters need to see that compliance no longer depends on aggressive adjustments or a single favorable collection week. A clean twelve-month record, restored liquidity, and consistent downside headroom can turn a distress narrative into evidence of disciplined governance; unsupported add-backs, recurring waivers, or unexplained forecast changes will instead increase pricing and reduce leverage capacity.
